Ecuador’s Fraught Mining Boom

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

  • In February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades.

Recent findings suggest that in February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades. The government tapped the military to protect strategic mining areas, extended mining contracts from 25 years to as long as 40 years, and replaced its rigorous environmental licensing system with an authorization process that allows projects deemed low impact to skip environmental review and citizen consultation.

Noboa argued that mining is Ecuador’s ticket out of poverty. The country is home to an estimated $220 billion of untapped mineral wealth—mostly gold, copper, and silver, according to the World Bank. But Ecuador has geochemically mapped just 30 percent of its territory, compared to 77 and 85 percent in neighboring Peru and Colombia, respectively. Ecuador’s two existing industrial mines didn’t begin large-scale extraction until 2019.

In February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades. The government tapped the military to protect strategic mining areas, extended mining contracts from 25 years to as long as 40 years, and replaced its rigorous environmental licensing system with an authorization process that allows projects deemed low impact to skip environmental review and citizen consultation.

Noboa argued that mining is Ecuador’s ticket out of poverty. The country is home to an estimated $220 billion of untapped mineral wealth—mostly gold, copper, and silver, according to the World Bank. But Ecuador has geochemically mapped just 30 percent of its territory, compared to 77 and 85 percent in neighboring Peru and Colombia, respectively. Ecuador’s two existing industrial mines didn’t begin large-scale extraction until 2019.

That is partly due to legal protections: Ecuador enshrined the rights of nature in its 2008 constitution, which requires environmental consultations and consent from affected Indigenous groups before major mining projects can begin. The constitution also allows communities to force referendums that can halt extractive projects.

According to recent reports, noboa wants to change that. His government has framed rolling back regulations and militarizing the sector as the path to dismantling illegal mining and bringing sustainable investment to Ecuador. Economists and security experts doubt that his policies can deliver on either front.

According to recent reports, “There are potentially massive benefits to [mining]. But there are massive costs, too,” said Monica DeBolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. If your objective is to have the benefits outweigh the costs, she said, “it all boils down to governance.” That has been a major issue for Noboa, who observers have accused of executive overreach.

Noboa was elected president in 2023. He kicked off his pro-mining agenda the next year, attending the world’s largest mining convention in Canada and leading a delegation that secured investment commitments in Ecuador worth nearly $5 billion from companies in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

After the visit, Noboa used an executive decree to concentrate mining, environmental, security, and financial powers into a single presidential committee. He followed up in 2025 by reopening Ecuador’s mining registry for the first time in seven years and absorbing the Environment Ministry into the Energy and Mining Ministry.

Recent findings suggest that that October, Noboa signed another presidential decree, this time barring nonprofits from “obstruction or interfering” with legally authorized mining projects and requiring them to seek ministry approval for any social programs. He ended the year with yet another decree, handing Ecuador’s mining regulator broad control over concessions and royalties, making it easier for mining companies to move into fresh areas.

Recent findings suggest that the last decree laid the groundwork for the February overhaul: a sweeping mining reform that loosened environmental licensing, authorized military control of private concessions, and set the stage for a U.S.-backed crackdown on illegal mining. Throughout his time in office, Noboa has also invoked his fight against organized crime to declare states of emergency that curb civil liberties and expand military control over mining provinces.

Industry observers note that “No other government—including my own—has ever pushed mining so aggressively,” remarked Fernando Benalcázar, Ecuador’s former vice minister of mines, who was in office when Ecuador’s two existing large-scale mines—Fruta del Norte and Mirador—came online. Both are in the Amazon rainforest, near the border with Peru. Under Noboa, another six major projects are in various stages of development.

Sources indicate that ecuador’s mining sector generated a total of nearly 12,000 direct jobs through the fourth quarter of 2025, and some estimates project that the industry may create another 460,000 direct and indirect positions by 2030. Minerals, which produced a record $4.16 billion in export revenues in 2025, now fall just behind Ecuador’s other top non-oil exports: cacao, bananas, and shrimp.

Sources indicate that but Noboa’s determination to rewrite Ecuador’s mining landscape has put him on a collision course with the constitutional order. The political opposition has argued that Noboa’s policies have relied on sidelining regulatory institutions and local communities. In the words of legislator Verónica Iñiguez, the president’s agenda “put the rat in charge of guarding the cheese.”.

Industry observers note that noboa’s mining decrees have not yet faced direct judicial challenges, but Ecuador’s top court has curbed many of his emergency declarations. It has also agreed to hear a challenge to the February mining law brought by Indigenous and community organizations. The plaintiffs argue that the government violated the constitution by failing to consult Indigenous communities, authorizing military activity in ancestral territories, and weakening environmental safeguards.

Although they might promote investment in the short term, aggressive tactics like Noboa’s can backfire in the long term, according to analysts. When top-down mining policy meets resistance in the form of legal setbacks and popular opposition, it creates uncertainty that spooks investors.

According to recent reports, “If there’s one thing that investors hate, that one thing is uncertainty,” DeBolle said. “[Policies] at loggerheads with the country’s constitution—that’s a recipe for uncertainty.” The World Bank likewise emphasizes that strong, transparent, and independent government institutions are critical for resource-rich countries to capture and sustain the benefits of mining.

Mounting opposition has already forced Noboa’s government to backtrack on projects that it rushed through. In 2025, the government issued a license for Dundee Precious Metals’ Loma Larga gold-silver-copper mine, despite local resistance and environmental concerns. The site rests atop a fragile ecosystem and a crucial water source, and communities repeatedly voted against mining there. After the rushed approval, local authorities and residents mobilized—filing lawsuits, launching media campaigns, and organizing a “March for Water” with more than 100,000 participants.

In a recent development, noboa’s office declared in late September that it would revoke the mine’s license. The environmental ministry did so a week later.

Sources indicate that noboa’s push to fast-track mining permissions isn’t just a bid for investment. Paired with military operations against illegal mines, the government also casts approved mining projects as a security tool to weaken organized crime groups, which have pushed into the illegal mining sector over the past decade. By 2024, illegal mining was estimated to generate up to $1 billion a year for criminal groups in Ecuador.

It has been revealed that in March, Noboa confirmed that Ecuador and the United States would increase their cooperation to fight illegal mining and drug trafficking. By October, Ecuador’s military stated that it had destroyed more than 1,000 illegal mining camps so far this year. Authorities have not released official casualty figures, but according to local reporting, there have been at least three deaths and many more injuries in these operations.

Sources indicate that luis Córdova Alarcón, who heads a program on conflict and violence at the Central University of Ecuador, said that the logic at the heart of Noboa’s policy is backward. “Legal mining isn’t the opposite of illegal mining. It is its partner in crime,” he said.

Córdova, who described the militarized approach as a “smokescreen,” pointed to illegal extraction within legally granted mining concessions, including arrangements in which concession holders rent access to illegal miners. He also highlighted the formal sector’s role in laundering illegal gold and the  direct involvement of corrupt figures in the criminal economy. His conclusions are backed by the United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime (UNODC), which recently published a report concluding that legally registered corporations can “become involved in illegal mining in different ways,” including infiltration by organized crime groups.

It has been revealed that multinational companies bring their own risks, including corruption, tax evasion, weak ownership transparency, and community conflict, said Julia Yansura, the program director for environmental crime and illicit finance at the FACT Coalition, a Washington-based financial-transparency advocacy group. “I think some governments can’t accept or don’t see risk with these big mining companies. It’s like they’re totally blind to it,” she said.

Easing regulation may open the door to more opaque foreign companies and weaker safeguards, according to Yansura. Militarized crackdowns ignore this sort of illegal mining, targeting small-scale and informal operations tied to organized crime. Yet even when it comes to informal small-scale mining, research has shown militarized approaches to be ineffective in the long run.

According to recent reports, authorities “blow up machinery, harass local people, and then leave,” Yansura noted. “That doesn’t actually solve the problem.” In fact, such operations can push miners deeper into illegality, undermine trust in public authorities, and fuel conflict and corruption.

For governments to curb illegal mining and undermine organized crime, UNODC recommends increasing regulation rather than relaxing it, holding significant corporations criminally responsible for participating in or facilitating illegal mining activity, and empowering affected communities through democratic engagement.

Noboa is failing on that last front. His mining policies are part of a broader centralization of power that has weakened Ecuador’s democracy. Under the guise of combating illegal mining, Noboa’s administration has pushed through legislation that expands his emergency powers, reduces restrictions on using lethal force against civilians, increases state surveillance, centralizes executive control over protected areas, and targets financing for environmental nongovernmental organization.

Indigenous groups, human rights advocates, and environmental defenders say that Noboa’s administration has used these laws to go after individuals who oppose his mining policies. They point to recent criminal charges against water defenders, the violent police dispersal of anti-mining protests in the capital of Quito in February, and the conviction of at least 15 anti-mining protesters on criminal charges throughout the course of this year.

“Quite simply, what the Ecuadorian government is doing is rolling back rights and eroding the institutions meant to protect them,” Iñiguez noted.

Recent findings suggest that in August 2025, when Ecuador’s highest court challenged the constitutionality of some of the new laws, Noboa led a march on the court, and senior members of his administration called judges “enemies of the citizenry,” alarming observers. He defended the suspended security measures and his efforts to pressure Ecuadorian institutions as necessary to combat criminal gangs, telling a crowd at the march that “[w]e are here to pursue justice and peace.”.

A month later, when Ecuador’s powerful Indigenous movement CONAIE declared a nationwide strike triggered by the end of fuel subsidies, Noboa deployed the military to break up roadblocks, resulting in at least three civilian deaths, and vowed to prosecute protest leaders for terrorism under a upcoming statute. In October 2025, CONAIE called off the strike, citing fear of government violence.

Sources indicate that noboa’s aggressive approach initially appeared popular with a public preoccupied with crime. But that changed on Nov. 16, 2025, when Ecuadorians went to the polls to vote in a national referendum. In a surprise upset, Noboa lost all four questions that would have further concentrated power in the executive. The biggest rebuke was to his proposal to convene a constituent assembly: Voters rejected rewriting Ecuador’s environmentally protective constitution.

Continuing to push through mining policy at odds with Ecuador’s constitution may turn out to be Noboa’s Achilles heel. Polling showed a sharp decline in the president’s approval ratings in the first half of this year compared to 2025. “The decline stems directly from his failure to respect the mandate of the ballot box,” Iñiguez said.

Anastasia Austin is an award-winning investigative journalist covering politics, economics, environmental problems, and organized crime in Latin America. X: @nastia492.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that secure Solar Futures, a commercial solar contractor, will build a 313-kW solar power system at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, Virginia. Construction of the system is expected to start later this year at no cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year power purchase agreement with Secure Solar Futures.

  • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
  • Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a latest tune to follow.

On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

Trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

Sources indicate that in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

Sources indicate that critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on notable commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

Industry observers note that like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

Recent findings suggest that political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

In a recent development, the election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

Recent findings suggest that an election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

We need your help to stay independent.

The Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

Political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

Sources indicate that in a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

Industry observers note that “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

Recent findings suggest that the August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, stated that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

In a recent development, separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

In a recent development, ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

It has been revealed that the criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

According to recent reports, court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

It has been revealed that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Newly introduced Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

An escalating confrontation between the two constituent parts of Iraqi Kurdistan is threatening to tear the besieged region apart. Since 2006, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which fought a brutal civil war in the 1990s, have formed an uneasy alliance to govern the predominantly-Kurdish, autonomous region of northern Iraq. So far, the region and the alliance have survived a war with the Islamic State in 2014 and more than 1,000 attacks by Iran and its proxies since the start of 2026.

Now, however, a fight over the allotment of parliamentary seats and cabinet positions is pushing both parties toward a formal split. On Thursday, Nov. 5, the PUK formally withdrew from the region’s joint government. If the division worsens, it could damage the Iraqi Kurdistan’s hard-won autonomy, threaten international support, and create new difficulties for citizens in their everyday lives.

On Nov. 11, U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack told the Kurdish parties that the Trump administration’s advice was to “get over it.” Barrack also spoke to Kurdish officials from both the PUK and KDP that week and underlined the importance of a united Kurdistan Region. In response, Bafel Talabani, the head of the PUK, called on the KDP to “get over it.” In the coming weeks, the parties’ willingness to compromise will determine if they can overcome their differences and prevent the breakup of the autonomous region.

Sources indicate that under U.S. mediation, the KDP and the PUK reached an agreement in 2006 whereby the KDP would control the presidency in Kurdistan and the PUK would control the Iraqi presidency in Baghdad. But this strategic agreement came under pressure after the PUK started to lose parliamentary seats to smaller opposition parties in 2009. In 2013, the KDP won 38 seats out of 100 in the Kurdish parliament compared to only 18 for the PUK. Then, in 2018, the KDP also attempted to challenge the PUK’s hold on the Iraqi presidency.

At the same time, the PUK also faced an internal power struggle after the death of its leader, Jalal Talabani, in 2017. Eventually, Talabani’s son Bafel Talabani took over the party in 2022, while his rival and cousin, Lahur Talabani, was subsequently given a five-year prison sentence for allegedly plotting an assassination, which he denies.

According to recent reports, after elections in October 2024, the KDP again emerged as the largest party with 39 seats, as compared to 23 for the PUK. The KDP went on to argue that the allotment of cabinet roles and other government positions should reflect the parties’ respective seat shares, while the PUK maintained that they should be divided on a 50-50 basis, as stipulated in the 2006 agreement.

It has been revealed that as a result of this disagreement, the Kurdistan Region has been without a functioning parliament since late 2024. On Nov. 4, however, the KDP managed to reach the legal quorum of 51 seats in order to convene the Kurdistan Region’s parliament. Having secured this majority with the help of defectors from opposition parties and three PUK members, the KDP proceeded to elect a new Presidency Board.

It has been revealed that hoshyar Siwaily, the head of the KDP’s foreign relations office, told Foreign Policy that over the past two years, the KDP and PUK have held intensive negotiations on forming a new government. However, he noted that the negotiations between the two parties over the allocation of ministerial and senior government positions remained inconclusive, bringing the process to an impasse.

“The KDP was therefore compelled to form a parliamentary majority and reactivate the Kurdistan Parliament,” Siwaily noted.

Saadi Ahmed Pira, a member of the PUK’s political bureau, disputed this assessment, claiming that while negotiations were still underway, and the deadlock was close to being solved, the KDP unilaterally decided to call for a session of parliament.

“The KDP was able to get the required number of MPs to meet the required 50+1 quorum by means of compensating several of our MPs and some MPs from other parties with large amounts of money, in essence bribing them to buy their votes,” Pira noted.

Industry observers note that the KDP denied the PUK’s allegations. “Almost all members of the other parties who attended the session categorically denied any wrongdoing, including allegations that they had received financial favors from the KDP,” Siwaily stated.

In response to these developments, PUK leader Bafel Talabani said he was pulling out of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) administration and threatened to form his own government outside of the KRG if the KDP moved ahead with its upcoming parliamentary majority.

“You appoint a president of the region, we will appoint a president of the region. You appoint ministers, we will appoint ministers,” Talabani stated.

The KDP claims that it will do “everything in its power to prevent such a disastrous outcome.” On Nov. 9, KDP President Masoud Barzani called on the PUK to sit down with the KDP to end the political crisis in the region. So far, Talabani has publicly dismissed the statement as “not serious.”.

Industry observers note that both parties will now look to Baghdad for support. On Nov. 9, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, a leader within the KDP, met with the Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi. After his visit, Barzani stated that Baghdad had agreed to continue paying all salaries in the region through the KRG administration. Bafel Talabani also traveled to Baghdad on Nov. 12 to lobby for his party and met with Iraqi leaders, including Iranian-backed Iraqi factions.

The PUK filed a lawsuit in Iraq’s top court in Baghdad on Nov. 10 to annul the reactivation of the parliament. On Nov. 15, the court rejected a separate request to suspend the parliament, and it will have a hearing on Dec. 14 on whether to reduce the KRG’s powers to a caretaker government.

Mohammed A. Salih, a nonresident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, told Foreign Policy that neither side wants to preclude reconciliation. “Both have shown considerable flexibility and pragmatism by keeping the door open for further negotiations and a negotiated settlement,” he said, adding, “The PUK’s withdrawal of its ministers from the cabinet is a blow to the KRG, but it will not bring the government down.”.

Salih argued that a lasting break would run counter U.S. strategic interests in Iraq, particularly given ongoing concerns over Iranian influence. “Messaging from the U.S. side also suggests that Washington does not want to see the Kurdistan Region divided into two separate administrations,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, if divisions persist, the price will also be paid by normal citizens. Binar Faeq Karim, an affiliate researcher at the think tank London Dialogue, suggested residents of the region would face “more complicated governance, difficulties in coordinating public services and economic policy and greater uncertainty over salaries, revenues and relations with Baghdad.”.

Industry observers note that former U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith, who has had a close relationship with the Kurds for more than four decades, told Foreign Policy that “recreating two administrations, as existed in the 1990s, would undermine all that has been achieved [by the Kurds] to date.”.

“I understand bitter partisan differences—they exist in the U.S. as well—but it is sad when politicians allow them to threaten the very existence of Kurdistan,” Galbraith mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in Fresh Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

Recent findings suggest that and on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

According to recent reports, in 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

Industry observers note that put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

According to recent reports, but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

We need your help to stay independent.

Recent findings suggest that the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just said for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

It has been revealed that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

Sources indicate that when Salon introduced in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in upcoming ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Industry observers note that over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

According to recent reports, the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

Sources indicate that the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Industry observers note that thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

#19247. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
  • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
  • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide stated.

Sources indicate that king is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

According to recent reports, the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will patch the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling stated.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

According to recent reports, U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

China, however, may have already beaten Trump to the punch.

Recent findings suggest that right out of the gate, Chinese President Xi Jinping has signaled that his administration is willing to act as a counterweight to the White House’s increasingly provocative trade policies. On Tuesday, Beijing agreed to cut duties on a swath of Canadian exports, amounting to roughly $280 million in tariff relief. In exchange, Ottawa promised to extend remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by another two years.

“Stronger communication and cooperation between China and Canada will benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world,” Xi told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during talks in Shenzhen, China. This was their third meeting since Carney took power in 2025, and it marked Ottawa’s continued efforts to diversify its trade away from Washington.

China also pledged on Tuesday to provide Peru with $22.5 million in aid to address what is expected to be the devastating fallout of this year’s El Niño. Lima applauded the measure, with President Keiko Fujimori stressing that “China is very vital to us because it is our ​principal trading partner.”.

Peru is one of the many places in Latin America where Beijing and Washington have competed for influence. Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department disclosed that it has committed $4.5 million to help Peru modernize its main port at Callao, in a move seen as a direct counter to a Chinese-controlled megaport less than 50 miles away that opened in 2024.

Industry observers note that perhaps most notably, though, is China’s potential openness to converse with Japan. A war of words over Taiwan, coupled with Beijing’s rare-earth export controls, has plagued Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s tenure. However, during Tuesday’s ASEAN gathering in Manila, Takaichi shook hands with Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu. Although few words were exchanged, the fact that such an interaction occurred has raised hopes that Takaichi’s upcoming trip to Shenzhen may be more cordial than previously anticipated.

Yet Beijing’s biggest days may still be to come. On Wednesday, Xi will host Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks on nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. With Trump at his weakest point to date (entering his lame-duck term after sweeping midterm losses and a Nvidia spy scandal), experts anticipate that Xi will aim to capitalize on Trump’s rocky footing.

In a recent development, “Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency,” FP columnist Howard W. French argued.

It has been revealed that dirty bomb threat? Iran is actively planning for potential strikes on U.S. soil, seven U.S. officials told CNN on Tuesday. Whether Tehran will or even can execute such an attack is unclear, and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis has insisted that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Still, even the possibility of such an assault signals growing alarm that a peaceful end to the Iran war may be out of reach.

Industry observers note that CNN reported that, according to U.S. intelligence, Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. Sources told CNN that this is not an indicator of an imminent attack but rather is one of several options that Iran may be exploring. Iranian officials, however, denied the report, with chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calling it “false flags” and “war mongering.”.

It has been revealed that experts, meanwhile, insist that Tehran may not have the capabilities or the desire to carry out such a plot. “An Iranian dirty bomb in Washington would be very hard to pull off,” retired U.S. Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN. “They’d have to move uranium halfway around the world and have a team in place to set it off. I don’t think they’ll do it. The U.S. response would be overwhelming.”.

Industry observers note that trump expressed a similar notion on Tuesday. When asked about the CNN article, the U.S. president told reporters that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” were it to attack the United States homeland.

Crosshairs on Crimean bridge. Ukrainian forces launched a second strike on Tuesday at a strategic bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever,’” Ukraine’s military command said in a statement. “Now, part of the structure lies in the water.” The attack marked the second consecutive assault on the critical crossing in just two days.

Recent findings suggest that the Kerch Strait Bridge—often highlighted as one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects—is the only rail crossing between Russia and the Crimean territory. Moscow has repeatedly used the 12-mile road to transport military and civilian supplies to its troops as well as to exert control over Ukraine’s southern coast; the Kerch Strait acts as a chokepoint for naval access from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. In recent years, the route has also become a symbol of Russia’s yearslong occupation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized this week’s attacks on the bridge as the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes. Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed on Tuesday that the assault on Kerch Strait Bridge occurred in tandem with a massive Ukrainian drone operation; Moscow claimed to have intercepted 1,441 drones across 22 regions on Tuesday in one of Kyiv’s biggest such attacks yet.

It has been revealed that what is Belgrade’s future? Hundreds of people gathered outside Serbia’s National Assembly on Tuesday to cheer on the country’s new parliament, the first since the ouster of President Aleksandar Vucic. Led by the grassroots Student List movement, the inaugural session kicked off what is expected to be the long process of forming a government.

Nearly two years of student-led protests against one of Europe’s most staunchly populist regimes culminated in the opposition’s sweeping victory in parliamentary elections last month. Student List lawmakers dominated in the polls, winning 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly compared to the Vucic-led Serbian Progressive Party’s 103 seats. Vucic initially blamed foreign interference for his loss, without citing evidence, despite international observers noting that his party held an unfair advantage.

Recent findings suggest that now begins the difficult task of governing a country that has been led by Vucic for the past 14 years. On Tuesday, the Student List was expected to nominate university professor Aleksandar Cupic to be the country’s latest parliamentary speaker. After that, the grassroots movement will still have to choose a prime minister and hold a snap presidential election; the deadline for the latter expires at the end of this year.

It has been revealed that the end of Pope Leo XIV’s 12-day Latin America tour wrapped up this week with a painful surprise. While traveling in the popemobile before his final Mass in Peru on Monday, Leo was struck in the eye by a flying rosary. It is unclear who threw the prayer beads, as worshippers often toss gifts at the pope, who is known for his (usually) quick reflexes.

However, Leo has already shaken off the incident. “The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart—or maybe in your eye—but that mark the life of someone,” Leo remarked on Tuesday.

Industry observers note that SOLRITE and sonnen strategy to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

It has been revealed that “Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”.

Recent findings suggest that the system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”.

In a recent development, when a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

Sources indicate that “With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

It has been revealed that pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a latest government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

In a recent development, pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

Industry observers note that second, in two months’ time, Trump’s maneuverability will be eclipsed by a Democratic Congress that can defund the war. Third, though U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment attempt last week, his political future still hangs by a thread.

Even if the risk of war declines, this does not guarantee a greater likelihood of a deal. Key obstacles—including Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, the future of its enrichment program, a regional cease-fire, sanctions relief, and the political cost for Trump—make both reaching and maintaining an agreement challenging.

It has been revealed that the most likely scenario may turn out to be neither war nor peace, yet something altogether different from the economic blockade “middle path” that Trump chose earlier. In this scenario, Trump’s economic warfare and blockade would end up little more than words on paper. Trump would declare victory, reject both war and peace, withdraw the U.S. military, step away from the table, and insist that the blockade and sanctions remain in place while quietly allowing them to fade into irrelevance.

Sources indicate that this would set in motion a gradual loosening of the blockade, with sanctions enforcement quietly eroding. Bit by bit, Asian and Middle Eastern countries would ramp up trade and investment in Iran, far surpassing current levels. Out of this slow transformation, a delicate fresh equilibrium would take shape: Sanctions enforcement would remain just robust enough for the United States to insist the system is intact, yet lax enough to persuade Tehran not to upset the emerging status quo.

This Swiss-cheese scenario is the only walk-away option that could work. If Trump truly keeps the blockade and sanctions in place, then the United States and Iran would be locked in a relentless standoff, always teetering on the edge of conflict, just as they are now. This fragile balance would inevitably tip into another war, completely undermining the whole point of walking away.

To be clear, the Swiss-cheese scenario is suboptimal compared with a peace deal. A peace deal that would end 47 years of enmity, uphold nonproliferation goals, open the Iranian economy to U.S. companies, and stabilize the region would far better serve U.S. interests. But the walk-away option carries the benefit, from Trump’s perspective, of avoiding an agreement that would manifest the failure of his war, as the Islamabad Memorandum did in the view of its critics. He will find it attractive because his focus is no longer on how much he can get, but how much he can avoid giving.

Sources indicate that indeed, the Swiss-cheese option guarantees that, while none of the sides walks away with a complete victory, everyone sidesteps their worst nightmare. Trump escapes both a humiliating compromise and the quagmire of another needless war. Tehran, in turn, dodges the devastation that a joint U,S. and Israeli assault on its vital infrastructure and energy lifelines would unleash. And given the shift in favor of nuclear weapons among the Iranian public, Iranian decision-makers may also welcome de facto partial sanctions relief without having to give up their stockpile of enriched uranium or give other nuclear concessions.

In a recent development, even Israel might breathe easier, since its worst fear—a U.S.-Iran diplomatic breakthrough that could see old enemies reconcile—remains off the table, while the possibility of a future U.S.-Iran conflict still lingers. Israeli leaders will certainly view any loosening of the sanctions pressure as a loss, but it is still superior to a deal that undoes the sanctions architecture altogether. Moreover, Israel may calculate that the scenario still offers plenty of opportunities to tighten the sanctions or even escalate matters toward war.

In short, it’s neither side’s worst option, and everyone’s least-costly scenario.

Recent findings suggest that and while Israel may still hope for chances to escalate, the Swiss-cheese scenario could turn out to be unexpectedly resilient, even as it leaves the U.S.-Iran conflict unresolved. Should this uneasy balance persist until 2029, the next U.S. president will stand at a crossroads: reignite tensions in pursuit of a better deal or quietly embrace the status quo and turn attention to the many other pressing crises on the United States’ plate. To most presidents, this will be a rather simple choice.

Given Trump’s refusal to admit defeat, his dread of looking like a loser, his allergy to tangled diplomacy, his fixation on eclipsing former U.S. President Barak Obama’s Joint Comprehensive Strategy of Action, and Iran’s refusal to offer him an ego-saving escape, Trump may ultimately declare a false victory and settle for the Swiss-cheese walk-away—not because it’s the smarter move but because it’s the cheapest way out.

#19241. Cooperating With China on AI Control Is a Fantasy

Cooperating With China on AI Control Is a Fantasy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity?
  • Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, argued that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He calls for “building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman posted on X, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”.
  • Recent findings suggest that should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity? The Trump administration prefers a “let it rip” approach to winning the AI race. But a growing chorus of American tech titans want to slow down AI development so that risk prevention measures can catch up with the technology.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, argued that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He calls for “building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman posted on X, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”.

Recent findings suggest that should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity? The Trump administration prefers a “let it rip” approach to winning the AI race. But a growing chorus of American tech titans want to slow down AI development so that risk prevention measures can catch up with the technology.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, argued that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He calls for “building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman posted on X, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”.

However, the case for greater controls contains a major weakness: It rests on coordination with China. Amodei’s three-point plan for pacing AI, for example, will require “cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities.”.

Altman agreed. He noted, “Even if just the U.S. and China could agree on some shared standards and testing for development of this technology, I think that’d be a wonderful accomplishment that the two of them can deliver.”.

Jacob Coxon, who made international news when he resigned from Anthropic in September, said, “A race with China could be very bad and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination.”.

But coordinating with China is much easier stated than done. Chinese President Xi Jinping is not interested in negotiating controls on AI development, and even if he were, he could not be trusted to abide by them. Believing that we can work with Beijing is a tech-world fantasy rooted in a shallow understanding of geopolitics.

To be fair, Amodei wrote, “We must not be naïve here: the geopolitical stakes are so high that there will likely be stark limits on what can be achieved.” But he and other technologists do not seem to fully grasp the depth of the challenge. Washington cannot afford, therefore, to unilaterally restrain itself as Beijing races ahead.

Just like with Cold War-era nuclear arms control agreements, any AI restraints must be mutually binding and verifiable. But Beijing is not interested in negotiating binding restraints. Instead, Xi has criticized Western attempts to control AI. China’s AI diplomacy instead trumpets the technology’s potential for economic development, especially for the global south.

In response to Amodei’s proposals for coordinated controls, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance.”.

Moreover, China and other dictatorships might even have rational incentives to embrace—not control—AI applications that court catastrophic risk. They trust algorithms more than their own people. Humans do not always reliably carry out orders, but computers do. I’ve talked to experts who say that China’s military officers, for example, are worryingly optimistic about the benefits and controllability of AI-enabled weapons systems.

Industry observers note that further, even if Washington and Beijing could agree on mutual constraints, Beijing is unlikely to abide by them. Dictatorships in general—and China, in particular—tend to cheat on international agreements. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union regularly cheated on nuclear arms control agreements while dictatorships like Iran, Iraq, Libya, Syria, and North Korea have systematically violated their commitments under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

According to recent reports, turning to the case of China, Beijing joined the World Trade Organization only to systematically violate its principles by stealing intellectual property from the West. It used its position in the World Health Organization to obstruct an effective investigation into the origins of COVID-19. China makes a mockery of the United Nations Human Rights Council as it engages in crimes against humanity in Xinjiang. Xi promised former U.S. President Barack Obama in the Rose Garden that he would not militarize islands in the South China Sea, and then he turned around and did just that. The list goes on.

Recent findings suggest that china’s compliance with a upcoming AI regime is unlikely to be any better. How would new AI limitations be effectively verified and monitored? A new international agreement to control AI would likely mean that Western democracies restrain themselves as Communist China cheats covertly and races ahead.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. and allied diplomats can certainly work among themselves to conceive reasonable standards and to pursue talks with their Chinese counterparts. The United Nations can set up a new agency for AI coordination. But everyone should be realistic that these efforts will likely be empty talk shops unable to make real progress.

In the absence of an effective pathway for cooperation with Beijing, Washington’s best path is to push forward and win the AI race.

Sources indicate that to be sure, AI presents possible existential threats, from the AI-enabled development of advanced bio and cyber weapons to lethal autonomous weapons systems and even automated nuclear command and control. In principle, it would be desirable to have binding international guardrails to protect against such catastrophic risks.

But there are competing demands. Washington must also win the AI race. The United States has enjoyed technological leadership for so long—at least since the time of Thomas Edison—that it almost takes it for granted. The United States’ technological edge has provided enormous economic, military, soft power, and geopolitical advantages.

Now, China wants to claim these advantages for itself.

In a recent development, losing the AI race to China would be a disaster. AI superiority would allow China to dominate the battlefields and boardrooms of the future. As Trump has rightly argued, “If we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position.”.

Industry observers note that losing the AI race would also have enormous consequences for Western values. What would it mean for democracy and human rights, for example, if the world is dependent on a dictatorship for 21st-century technology? China could use the technology for espionage, sabotage, supply chain coercion, and censorship. Could we even use Chinese-built AI tools to search for Tiananmen Square in the future? What else would be off limits?

With the stakes this high, the United States cannot afford to compete with one hand tied behind its back. By securing AI leadership, Washington will be in a much stronger position to force China to play its game and negotiate future AI guardrails from a position of strength.

Industry observers note that as Trump said, “We’re leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way. I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution.”.

It has been revealed that it is unfortunate that Washington does not have a more reliable negotiating partner in Beijing. But given that reality, the least bad feasible path forward for now is to let it rip.
