📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders matter new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Industry observers note that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus highlights no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is exacerbated by an underfunded health system and armed conflict in eastern provinces, where global mining projects have led to increased disease transmission.

Recent findings suggest that the outbreak is “still serious, and is still not under control,” said Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. The death toll since the outbreak began in May has passed 5,500 people, with more than 11,000 people infected, according to Congolese government figures released last week.

Infections are now spreading at double the rate as when the outbreak began, according to Kaseya. More than 80 percent of fresh cases are emerging outside of known contact lists, and more than 65 percent of deaths have occurred outside of healthcare facilities, he added.

Kaseya called the lack of coordination between Congo’s government and foreign donors “a collective failure,” urging donors to release $1.6 billion in pledged aid.

International donors have disbursed more than $962 million to organizations that are implementing Congo’s Ebola response. But around $700 million of that sum was unaccounted for as of last month, according to Kaseya. The Africa CDC noted that it was too early to attribute this discrepancy to embezzlement, but an investigation is underway.

In 2020, Congo’s former health minister was convicted of embezzling more than $400,000 from funds intended to fight Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak.

Meanwhile, Congolese health workers—who have not been paid for months—have gone on strike. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned last week that ambulances had run out of fuel, staff were untrained, and that the Congolese government and United Nations agencies needed to “strengthen oversight and accountability.” MSF has called the outbreak “out of control.”.

For Congo, dealing with the Ebola crisis requires tackling systemic problems beyond healthcare, including poverty, conflict, and inefficient governance. But Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi appears to be focused on cementing his grip on power. On Nov. 9, he signed a law that critics say could grant him a third term in office.

Recent findings suggest that congo’s 2006 constitution allows a maximum of two presidential terms and explicitly prevents parliament from changing those rules under any circumstance. The new law lowers the threshold for holding national referendums and permits constitutional overhauls through referendums “in case of absolute necessity.”.

Tshisekedi became president in January 2019; his second term ends in 2028. He has stated that he is not seeking a third term but would serve one if given a mandate by voters. “I have not asked for a third term, but I tell you this: If the people want me to have a third term, I will accept,” Tshisekedi said in May.

On Nov. 1, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a new rebel alliance led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, sent a letter to U.S. officials and the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo warning that any constitutional changes could derail peace negotiations. Kabila’s alliance includes the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration negotiated a peace accord between Congo and Rwanda in December 2025 that seemed to prioritize securing U.S. access to Congo’s critical minerals over tackling domestic government reforms and bolstering a weak state. Expanded mining in Congo’s forests has increased human contact with animals that carry the Ebola virus, according to scientists.

Nearly one year on, amid an Ebola outbreak and on the precipice of further conflict, Congo is paying the price for the institutional neglect enshrined in the deal.

Industry observers note that wednesday, Nov. 18: An Egyptian court hears the retrial of Lina Attalah, the editor in chief of Mada Masr, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The U.N. has described the charges against Attalah as an assault on press freedom.

Recent findings suggest that the U.N. Security Council hears a briefing from the International Criminal Court on its work in Libya.

In a recent development, thursday, Nov. 19, to Saturday, Dec. 19: Dak’Art, the biennale of contemporary African art, returns to Dakar, Senegal.

Industry observers note that wednesday, Nov. 25: The U.N. Security Council is due to renew its sanctions targeting al-Shabaab and other armed groups in Somalia.

In a recent development, amnesty report on South Sudan. A upcoming report from Amnesty International accuses South Sudan’s government and U.N. peacekeepers of failing to act on advance warnings of a March massacre that killed more than 200 people. The report came ahead of an announcement that South Sudan would again delay general elections to February 2027.

According to recent reports, the elections were previously scheduled for Dec. 22. The South Sudanese government did not cite a reason for the move, but authorities have repeatedly pushed back elections since 2022 amid a power struggle between President Salva Kiir and his ousted former deputy, Riek Machar.

Sources indicate that A 2018 power-sharing arrangement between Kiir and Machar  broke down last year after an attack on a military base in Upper Nile state by an armed group known as the White Army, which killed more than 250 soldiers. Kiir accused Machar and his party’s military wing of colluding with the White Army, which Machar denied.

Machar is presently on trial for charges including treason.

According to recent reports, cape Verde elections. Cape Verdean President José Maria Neves was reelected on Sunday, capturing more than 63 percent of the vote amid record low turnout, according to provisional results. Neves’s main challenger, former Justice Minister Joana Rosa—the country’s first woman presidential candidate—conceded on Monday.

The lack of opportunities for young people in Cape Verde was a major election topic. Rosa pledged to address complications facing young people, while Neves promised to organize a summit to address youth emigration. According to data released in July by Cape Verde’s statistics body, around 65 percent of people aged 15 to 35 said they intended to emigrate.

Neves’s party has dominated Cape Verdean politics since it gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

Madagascar’s ties to Russia. U.S. Africa Command’s deputy commander, John Brennan, warned against Madagascar’s strengthening ties with Russia last week, saying that Moscow is importing the “Sahel model” to the island.

Industry observers note that “We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent,” Brennan mentioned in a media briefing. Since the country’s 2025 coup, Russia has supplied the military-backed government with weapons—amid repeated calls from young Madagascans for a return to democracy.

Recent findings suggest that some Africans perceived Brennan’s comments as lecturing from the United States. “America is not talking to Russia as a partner. It is talking to Madagascar as a client,” Fortune Madondo wrote in Modern Ghana, suggesting that the United States might condition assistance to needy Madagascar on its allegiance.

The criticism underscored why it’s vital that U.S. officials consider how their comments land in Africa. If not framed carefully, they could play into Russia’s narrative that the United States is acting like a colonial power.

Industry observers note that ghana to boost local manufacturing. Ghana will invest $10 billion over four years in a domestically funded “latest economy” program to boost local manufacturing and jobs. Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told parliament in his 2027 budget speech last Friday that the funds will increase refining capacity and reduce lower-value raw materials exports.

Sources indicate that around $1.5 billion of the package will be allocated to financing refining facilities for gold, manganese, bauxite, and lithium. The Ghanaian government stated it is relying on tax reforms already approved by parliament, better tax collection, and revenue from oil and minerals exports to finance the program.

The winner of this year’s 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza, has been cleared of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, “The Blue Fighter,” after an October article in the Atlantic said that the AI detection software Pangram found the story was entirely AI-generated.

The Atlantic article sparked pushback from Africa’s literary community. Critics said AI detection tools are disproportionately weaponized against authors from marginalized backgrounds. Following a monthlong review, the Caine Prize’s board said that digital forensic evidence revealed the article was human-written and that Kundizeza’s $13,000 award stands.

Nigeria’s surveillance state. An investigation by Ajibola Amzat for the Center for Collaborative Investigative Journalism found that Nigeria has spent billions of dollars of public funds on surveillance technology that is supposedly intended to fight insecurity—but is routinely used instead to monitor protesters, journalists, and government critics.

“Constitutionally guaranteed dissent is being watched and increasingly hunted while the terrorists and bandits freely operating in several corners of Nigeria’s 36 states remain elusive,” Amzat wrote.

Europe’s externalized borders. On Monday, five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands—revealed intends to send asylum-seekers who have exhausted all legal avenues to Rwanda.

Industry observers note that in 2024, the United Kingdom scrapped a similar deal due to legal challenges over the country’s human rights record. Since 2019, the European Union has also funded a scheme operated by the U.N. refugee agency that temporarily evacuates refugees from Libya to Rwanda.

In light of this week’s news, we’re revisiting Sally Hayden’s 2020 Foreign Policy dispatch from Rwanda’s refugee centers. “At what point does the EU become responsible for refugees it has forced from its borders through externalization policies?” Hayden wrote at the time.

In a recent development, eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

In a recent development, democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Ueland stated if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

Democrats said Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

Industry observers note that democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

Ueland did not give a direct response.

In a recent development, “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he remarked. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

Sources indicate that “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters stated. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

“That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

Ueland remarked his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland mentioned he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

For example, he stated GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland remarked he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland remarked, “To be clear, yes.”.

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, stated he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

According to recent reports, paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

Recent findings suggest that and he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” mentioned Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, noted by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

He stated GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

In a recent development, the union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
  • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
  • Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

In a recent development, lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

Sources indicate that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 new nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-introduced ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

Sources indicate that then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-launched long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant upcoming capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan problem stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

Industry observers note that the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

Recent findings suggest that beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

According to recent reports, china hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby stated, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-rolled out cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

It has been revealed that A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses new warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

Beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

Sources indicate that chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

It has been revealed that the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more vital, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

Sources indicate that exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

Sources indicate that another crucial step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

In a recent development, ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

The 65-page report, titled "China's Wingmen: How Western Government Policy Enabled China's Rise in the Skies," follows a year-long investigation by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, led by Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Ranking Member Ro Khanna, D-Calif. China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) is the country's military, which the committee indicates has benefited from civilian aerospace technology transfers.

"American and European companies transferred technology to China that could be used against our brave men and women in uniform. With the CCP’s military-civil fusion there are no private companies in China," Moolenaar said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN.

The bipartisan panel examined at least six U.S.-China joint ventures involving American defense suppliers GE Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace and RTX subsidiary Collins Aerospace.

Investigators found that GE transferred foundational avionics technology to a joint venture with a subsidiary of AVIC, the Chinese state-owned conglomerate that develops military aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter. RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER.

What India Makes of Trump’s Asia Trip

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

It has been revealed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday. Australia, India, Japan, and the United States announced initiatives including cybersecurity collaboration, a cable connectivity framework, and a maritime surveillance exercise.

The Quad meeting likely brought some relief for Upcoming Delhi. The grouping is important for India’s foreign-policy interests, bringing together some of its closest security partners in an effort to counter China. (However, the Quad states rarely mention Beijing in their public messaging about the grouping to avoid antagonizing the superpower.).

Though India has engineered a rapprochement with China in the last two years, taking steps to reduce border tensions and scale up trade and investment, they remain bitter strategic rivals. India prioritizes opportunities to work multilaterally to push back against China’s power through non-security collaborations in areas such as technology and infrastructure investment.

Scheduling problems and U.S.-India tensions have prevented high-level Quad engagement since September 2024. Quad supporters will point to Tuesday’s meeting as an indication of the grouping’s resilience, much like how it bounced back from quiescence in 2017—interestingly, with another summit in Manila when each member’s ties with China faced increasing strain.

Still, the Quad remains mired in uncertainty, mainly because of U.S. President Donald Trump. His administration’s signaling about taking a softer approach to competition with China, coupled with silence about the fate of the U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy, suggests that the current White House may not be prepared to throw its full support behind the Quad.

Though an incoming Democratic Congress might take a tougher line on China, this is unlikely to shape the Trump administration’s thinking on the Quad. As a result, the wider ASEAN summit arguably held more immediate significance for New Delhi than the Quad meeting.

Recent findings suggest that indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long sought to step up India’s game in Southeast Asia—a region home to key Indian partners and multiple growing economies. India has especially strong incentives to ramp up engagement given China’s large footprint there. In that sense, the stakes were high for Modi’s engagement with ASEAN leaders this week.

In a recent development, new Delhi will now closely watch as Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. There is a lack of clarity, but the discussion will reportedly include the Iran war and nuclear nonproliferation.

According to recent reports, such themes are unlikely to concern India, which has a strong interest in the wars in both Iran and Ukraine coming to an end. But the summit will be a vindication of sorts for New Delhi. In 2025, Trump slammed a meeting among Modi, Xi, and Putin in China; now, he is coming to the same table.

However, the boost that China is likely to get from the trilateral isn’t ideal for India. The U.S., Chinese, and Russian leaders have never had such a formal face-to-face exchange. Beijing’s capacity to convene the three leaders, against a backdrop of long-standing U.S.-Russia hostility, is a major diplomatic achievement.

In a recent development, for Latest Delhi, the biggest takeaway from this week’s high-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen is that the Quad leaders’ meeting was a relative sideshow. The ASEAN and APEC summits will generate more attention and hold more immediate significance for Indian policymakers.

Bangladesh cleared for DFC investment. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC) announced on Monday that Bangladesh was now eligible to receive its financing. The DFC, which mobilizes private investment, has taken on added importance since the demise of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) last year.

Until now, Bangladesh was ineligible for DFC financing because of U.S. concerns about labor conditions in the country. Negotiations between Washington and Dhaka to address these concerns and clear the way go back to the Biden administration.

Industry observers note that the announcement couldn’t come at a better time for Bangladesh, which faces serious development challenges and severe economic stress. Some of its most pressing challenges—such as fuel shortages and the world’s worst measles epidemic—are tied to energy and healthcare, two of DFC’s priority areas for investment.

It has been revealed that DFC-funded projects could bring a boost to U.S.-Bangladesh relations. Development cooperation, for years embodied by the large USAID mission in Dhaka, has long been a major component of the relationship.

Khan issues plea for medical treatment. Lawyers for Imran Khan sent an open letter on Monday from the jailed former prime minister to top judges in Pakistan, imploring them to secure better healthcare for Khan and his wife, who is also in prison. In the letter, Khan notes he is suffering from high blood pressure and is at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

For months, Khan’s lawyers, family, and supporters have noted his health is worsening, while officials say he is stable and regularly monitored by prison doctors. In August, Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered Khan to be transferred to a private hospital for an extended period; he was instead brought to a government hospital and only briefly.

Concern for Khan’s health was one reason why leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party revealed nationwide protests last month. But aside from some demonstrations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the only one governed by the PTI, the campaign didn’t materialize. The party might be back-channeling with the country’s leadership to secure concessions for Khan.

British royals visit India. The United Kingdom’s Prince William and Princess Catherine completed a three-day visit to India on Wednesday. They began their trip in Mumbai, where they participated in the Earthshot Prize ceremony. William founded the award, which focuses on developing latest solutions to climate change.

Sources indicate that the royal couple then traveled to New Delhi, where they met Modi. Their visit underscores the strong ties between India and its former colonizer. U.K.-India relations have deepened in recent years, buoyed most recently by a free trade deal that formally entered into force in July.

It has been revealed that for that matter, U.K.-Pakistan ties are also quite warm; William and Kate made a visit there in 2019. Deep people-to-people ties, thanks in part to large Indian and Pakistani diasporas in the U.K., help bolster these relationships. British colonial rule may have left a problematic legacy in the subcontinent, but diplomacy today is in a good place.

In a recent development, newly introduced Delhi hosts an arts and culture forum this weekend under the banner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). The idea for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum came from India, which will head the event even though Pakistan is the current SCO chair. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, will travel to New Delhi to represent Islamabad.

With India-Pakistan ties so tense in recent years, the rare occasions when senior ministers from one country have traveled to the other have mostly come in their capacity as SCO members.

Industry observers note that pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari traveled to India for an SCO summit in 2023, while Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar went to Pakistan the next year. Malik’s visit, however, comes at an especially fraught moment, with the relationship essentially frozen since the brief military conflict between India and Pakistan in 2025.

In a recent development, looking ahead, a big question is whether Modi will travel to Pakistan for the SCO leaders’ summit scheduled for next August. Modi visited Pakistan in December 2015, early in his first term. Several days after his trip, Pakistani terrorists attacked an Indian Air Force base. Since that incident, Modi’s government has taken an especially hard line toward Pakistan.

Even though Jaishankar went to Pakistan in 2024, it is unlikely that Modi himself will make the trip next year—especially if the protest movement against his government that has gripped India in recent months remains active.

In the Daily Mirror, writer K.K.S. Perera analyzes Sri Lanka’s new budget: “Has the 2027 Budget adequately addressed the economic difficulties confronting ordinary Sri Lankans? The answer must be examined against people’s actual living conditions rather than the Government’s financial projections, development promises, and announcements.”.

Industry observers note that in the Print, education expert Archana Dalmia reflects on Italian-born Indian politician Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir, Belonging. “Destiny had written a very different story from the one she could ever have imagined,” she writes. “Through love, loss and the unexpected turns of life, she became part of a country that was once so distant from her own.”.

Industry observers note that in Dawn, public health specialist Muhammad Aftab Gohar argues the urgency of eliminating rabies in Pakistan. “The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” he writes. “A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.”.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)

Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from left, Sens.
  • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
  • It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, from left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission upcoming authority over interstate transmission lines.

It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately noted they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

The "major four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

"This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito noted before passage.

Ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

In a recent development, the Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, initiative and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., noted last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as currently drafted.

However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an matter: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the newly introduced Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

Recent findings suggest that merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both mentioned the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

"I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote Thursday night.

It has been revealed that but Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental issues under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

Industry observers note that as part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

#19191. Why Israel Is Losing America

Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.
  • American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

According to recent reports, as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

It has been revealed that things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a upcoming paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Industry observers note that whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

According to recent reports, time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace proposal for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he stated himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Recent findings suggest that trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

According to recent reports, unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, unveiled wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Sources indicate that without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

It is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

In a recent development, israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s plan for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

According to recent reports, israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of latest Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Sources indicate that israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

Industry observers note that these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

National Police Association spokesperson and retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, raises concerns over Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposal to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group in an interview with Fox News Digital.

EXCLUSIVE: A retired police sergeant with nearly three decades of law enforcement experience warned that she would not bring her own family to New York City amid Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to dismantle a specialized NYPD unit responsible for counterterrorism support and crowd control.

"I wouldn't take my family there right now," retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokesperson for the National Police Association, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Smith's warning follows Mamdani's announcement that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a roughly 500-officer specialized unit involved in counterterrorism, major event security and protest response, will be disbanded as part of a broader overhaul of how the nation's largest police department handles demonstrations.

MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS.

"One of the beauties of this strategic response group is that these are a group of officers who are used to working together," Smith noted. "They train together. They have specialized knowledge of how to deal quickly and safely with these types of situations, including an active shooter.".

Smith warned that breaking up the specialized unit could create vulnerabilities if its responsibilities were redistributed without preserving existing operational relationships.

The overhaul also imposes newly introduced restrictions on police tactics during protests, including prohibitions on long guns and tear gas, according to the mayor's office.
